title: An idiv that leaves division by zero to the host, proved to throw exactly there
summary: The interpreter's `idiv` checks for a zero divisor and throws `ArithmeticException` before dividing on the host. A developer notices that the host is itself a JVM, whose division throws the same exception on the same input, and removes the check from `idiv` and `irem`. The property committed for each kernel now declares the exceptional behaviour as JML does, `throws: ArithmeticException when divisor == 0`, instead of assuming the zero divisor away; the prover covers the exceptional path with the normal one and proves that the host throws exactly where the check did.

change.description: Remove the explicit zero check from `idiv` and `irem` and return `dividend / divisor` and `dividend % divisor` directly; the comment says that the host's own `idiv` throws the `ArithmeticException` the instruction requires. The tests for rounding, the sign of the remainder, the division identity and division by zero pass.

risk: Whether a check is redundant depends on what the code under it does on the inputs the check excluded, and a reviewer reading `dividend / divisor` has to know that Java's `/` throws `ArithmeticException` on zero (it does), that it throws nothing on `Integer.MIN_VALUE / -1` (it does not; JLS §15.17.2), and that the exception's class is the one the guest program's `catch` will name (it is). A port of this kernel to a host whose division traps, or returns an unspecified value, would make the same cleanup a silent miscompilation of every guest program that catches `/ by zero`. The tests cover division by zero with one input each for `idiv` and `irem`.
explanation: Until this change the property of `idiv` was stated under `assume: divisor != 0`, which is the usual way to keep an exception out of a property and leaves the exceptional path to the tests. The property now has a throws clause, `throws: ArithmeticException when divisor == 0`, JML's `signals`: on the inputs where the condition holds the method must throw that exception, and everywhere else it must return and the assertion must hold. The tool compiles the clause into the generated harness as a handler for the declared class, caught before the generic ones, and an `expected` flag computed before the call, and asserts that the two agree; JBMC proves both paths of the patched `idiv` in a fraction of a second, as it does `irem`. The proof says what the reviewer had to know: the host's division throws exactly on zero, an `ArithmeticException` and not a subclass of something else, and on `Integer.MIN_VALUE / -1` it returns the dividend, which the assertion's `divisor != -1 || result == -dividend` still pins down. The exceptional path is no longer assumed away: a future `idiv` that throws on some other input, or returns on zero, fails the same property.
resolution: Merge. The throws clause stays as the kernel's specification of its exceptional behaviour, in the file the build proves; the tests for division by zero stay as documentation, and no longer carry the check alone.
notes: The throws clause of the property brings the exceptional path under the proof.
Leaving division by zero to the host throws exactly where the removed check did. Compare 034, the unsafe change on the same method.
provenance: Constructed from JVMS §6.5 (`idiv`, `irem`), which specifies `ArithmeticException` on a zero divisor, and the observation that the host of this interpreter is a JVM.

references.title: JVMS §6.5, idiv: if the value of the divisor is 0, idiv throws an ArithmeticException
JLS §15.17.2, Division Operator /: the integer division that overflows, and the ArithmeticException on zero
JML reference manual, method specifications: the signals clause, which states when a method throws and what holds then
